From Belt's Weekly Messenger, London November 13, 1843. FRANCE. His Majesty Louis Philippe accompanied bv Marshal Soult, inspected on the previous day the Paris fortifications. M. Descharrieris, Lieut. Colonel of the Engineers, who had the management of Noisyle Secfort, committed suicide on Tuesday. A statement having appeared to the effect that letters had been received from l'ondicherrv. mentioning, that the Governor of the isle of Bourbon had taken possession of the islands of Amsterdam and St. Paul, and had placed garrisons in them, the Journal du Havre throws discredit upon the statement. It professes to have received intelligence from Bourbon of the 12th of August, in which no mention whatever of such an occurrence was made. It could not, therefore, have been known at Pondicherry on the 20th. unless the expedition had returned to the coast of Coromandel, instead of returning to the place whence it set out. The folly of such a proceeding as that of taking possession of uninhabited rocks in the midst of the sea, out of the ordinary track, and known only as a point of observation to ships steering for the south of New Holland, would appear to confirm this impression. SPAIN. The most important feature in the news from Spain this week is the revolutionary movement in the important sea-port town of Vigo. The opposition papers in Madrid contain accounts of this movement, and anticipate that it will rapidly spread through the whole of Galicia. The Esparterist general, Jriarte, had the command of the National Guards, who have declared in favour of the

Central Junta. The movement took place on the 22d ult , and on the 4th inst., the date of the latest advices, the town was in a state of blockade, the National Guard, under the command of General Iriarte, being prepared to defend the place against the Captain General of Galicia, who was advancing against it with 4000 troops of the line. The Captain General had ordered her Majesty's Consul to leave Vigo and proceed to the small town of Congas, on the north side of the Vigo Bay, and at his request had conveyed him to that town. It is said that 12,000 muskets had been landed. An attempt at insurrection had been made at Seville, which was repressed bv the energy ol the authorities. A number of persons bad been arrested, and amongst others several soldiers and officers of the garrison Olivenca, a strong place on the frontier of Portugal, was also said to have pronounced in favour of the Central Junta. Some sensation has been created in Gibraltar, Algesiras, and the neighbouring parts of Andalusia, by the arrival of General Nogueras. Espartero's late War Minister at Gibraltar, direct from London. Letters from Algesiras announced some apprehension of intrigues in the interest of the Ayacuchos, which Nogucras was said to be promoting at Gibraltar in conjunction with the Spanish Consul Llanos.
EGYPT. Letters from Alexandria announce that the Viceroy of Egypt had given orders to place 40,000 men immediately under arms, in order h) reduce the i'asha of Soudan to obtdiencc,

this officer having declared himself independent of Mehemel Ali. Ahmed, Pasha oi Soudan isstated t« bealiout 45 years of age, of remarknble sang ft oid, and brave as u lion. In fiis youth he was purchased, with other Citcassian slaves, by Mebemet Ali. He was brought up as a soldier, and was enrolled in the first regular regiment ever raisedin Egypt. He first served in Arabia and the Hedjaz, was promoted to the rank of colonel, and subsequently sent to Canada, and finally to St Jean d'Acre, where he particularly distinguished himself for his brilliant courage. þÿ He followed the fate of the Egyptian army in Syria, his regiment having been ever dis tinguished for its bravery and discipline. In the year 183t> he was made minister of war at Cairo. The 1'asha wished lo deduct front the pay of the army all the expenses of aims and artillery which had been consumed in the wars of Syria. Ahmed was of a contrary opinion, and expressed himself in the follow ing terms: þÿ "After having exposed their lives, should the troops pay for the mateiials consumed ! impossible I" 'i'liis obset ration was sufficient to cause his disgrace. He was ordered to confine himself to his house, but he was beloved by the entire ainiy, and was finally appointed Pasha of Soudan, þÿ a species of honourable exile. The revolt of Ahmed fias caused Alehemet Ali serious uneasiness, lie cause in attacking Ahmed he attacks tnu Porte.

Pride is a gentlemanly failing, and sins sweetly and respectably. It smells of civet, and turning its varnished elite k to the sun, walks abroad in purple and fine linen, Nav, it rides in a coach and four; and in j hours of penitential castigation, bolls itsell in a pew ol best upholstery, and in a lit of humility lasting at least a couple of hours, calls itself a miserable sinner, Hence, pride at its worst has its good graces. Covetousness and avarice are called vices; for oor part, we have thought them amongst the noblest virtues. And so, indeed in their heart of hearts, do nine men out often think them. And this is what they do; they give them hard names, and then, to make amends for

the seeming haishness, take them to their bosoms; in the same way that a foolish mother, when she sees her hairy doing all soi is of misdemeanors, ci ies you little wretch, and then catches the child in her arms, and c on r it with kisses There arc a few other vices that mav all of them fie turned into passable virtues, if they he found in good company. Lust, cruelty, selfishness, each and all of these may have a pietty alias another trilling musical name for the long ears of biped tliistic eaters. But there is one vice þÿ and that vice is poverty þÿ which all rntn declare to he infamous, incorrigible, incapable of amendment ; a leper þÿ a wretch, a monster-to he c< nfined in cabins and cellars, or sent like a scape goat into the howling wilderness. þÿ Hunch.

This convenient and we may add necessary establishment is we are most happy to announce completed, and allhough a minor undertaking still as a specimen that the public mind is awakened to objects of general utility, we think it highly satisfactory. Sea Bathing in a tropical climate is eminently conducive to the preservation of the general Health, it braces the system, it equalizes the circulation, it imparts an elasticity to the mind and is besides a most innocent and pleasant recreation. Unfortunately it cannot always be indulged in safety, on account of those pesls of the ocean, yclept, Jack Sharks, hut in a building of this description guarded by piles the scallv monsters may look on but cannot bile, anil the conviction of its personal safely will impart an additional zest to its enjoyment: we should like however to see it neatly painted and ihe galleries enclosed bv lattice woik, we would in fact prefer its being made a little more ornamental, we should also like to see another one erected for the use of ladies and children ; sea bathing is the most efficient remedy and preventive for that languid debili-

INI) I The Indian mail of the 1st of November . has arrived. The intelligence which it brings O is of considerable interest. The affairs of Punjuab continue to engross public attention. This heterogeneous kino-dom, which was conquered by Rurjeet Singh hv means of Ihe European officers whom he emplosed in his service, is now on the verge of dissolution. Four Kings have ruled it since 183!), and the age of the present Sovereign is but seven years, and even his legitimacy is questioned, for he is publicly said not to be the son of Runjeet, which fact was pretended by Dhyan Singh, in order to conciliate tho good will of the enthusiastic adherents of the þÿ Old Lion of Lahore,'

ST. © SJ © S iT33 Every newspaper reader knows the cause of the death of Runjeet, his continued debauchery, of Kurruck Singh, his debility aud treachery, of Neo Nehal Singh from the contrivance of those who wished to remove the most daring object of Kunjeet's descen dan's from the road of their ambition ; and finally the assassination of Shore Singh, by Ajeet Singh, who was excited thereunto by the þÿl rime Minister Dhyan Singh, whom he murdered soon after the assassination of his master. Ajeet Singh was afterwards overcome by the son of Dhyan Singh, whose name is Heera Singh, and who lias been reported to have been also slain, although noihing certain appears to be known on the subject. It is useless to attempt to describe the wretched state of Lahore. It resembles Rome, when rich with the spoils of all the world and drank with every sensual pleasure, it frequently became the prey of every unlicensed body of soldiers whose General had the command.

The Akalees, a set of violent enthusiasts, who live by bullying all classes under pretence of superior sanctity, will also contribute to ensure the ptogtess of t he revolution. þÿ Ihe soldiers are now demanding the most exorbitant pay, and they assume the right of dismissing their officers. The death of Holkar, an enervated and dissipated ruler, took place at Indore on the 24th of October, He tiad passed many yeats as a prisoner, and was almost incapable of reigning. An adopted child, aged i) years, is Ids successor. The British Resident, JSir Claude Martin Wade, has arranged matteis so that no confusion is apprehended during the long minority. CHltN A.

The news from China is to the 2Sth of August. The state of business, with the exception of the coast ng trade, does not appear satisfactory at Hong Kong, so that many of the merchants declined going there. Sick ness existed there to a considerable extent. Opium was not to be protected by the British and yet the smuggling continued to prosper. The Bogue forts were rebuilt in nearly the same state as before. The Chinese Government had claimed 4,000,000 dollars from the Hong merchants as a contribution on account of the Canton ransom. 'I he Emperor had issued several proclamations, exhibiting a wish to protect þÿ the foreign barbarians " and to punish those officers who had maltreated the sailors that were ship-wrecked in the Nerbudda and Anna in the beginning of 1842. St. Croix, Ciiristianstcd (Monday) January 22, 1814, Mild and equal la xv >, promptly anil Itumnnelv executed, are justly considered among the greatest blessings any people can enjoy ; at the same time they are an indication of the depravity of the human heart. Were all mankind honest and upright, there would he no need of locks and holts, of prisons and fetters, of laws and courts, of judgments and executions; if every one followed that golden precept promulgated by the Divine Founder of All-good þÿ to do by others as we would that they should do by þÿus, we should all sit down in safety under our own vines and lig trees, with none to disturb our tranquillity, or make us afraid. Hut in the present lapsed and sinful state of mankind, when the greater part are disposed to do evil and not good io their neighbors, it is necessary for the peace and security oi society that the wicked p o pensities of our heat Is should be restrained by good and wholesome laws and regulations, whose infraction in order to render them efficacious, must be strictly and severely punished Yet the warning that is given by the þÿlaw s, and the terror that is held out l>v punishments, are insufficient to prevent the commission of crimes. The malefactors Bob alias Robert and Abel belonging to Instate Mount Stewart suffered for the death of their fellow servant. They were accused for having feloniously, bv poison, caused his death ; appeared before a court of inquiry, and condemned. They were, accordingly on Saturday morning last, jri the town of Frederikstcd, summoned on the

scaffold to appear before a just God to render a rigorous account ot their wicked propensities ; the signal was given, the scaffold dropped. and in a lew minutes they were launched into eternity. They remained hanging during the whole day. We can give little sympathy to these sufferers þÿ the offence for which they were punished was rewarded in a becoming manner. May their fate be a warning to deter others irom using poison on a slight provocation, and with slight reason, for no man has a right to destroy the life of his fellow creature ! !

The great point of interest was the decision of Lord Ellenborough relative to the proceedings to be adopted towards that country. In a political view the advantages of possessing the Funjaub are incalculable ; it is there where nature appears to have established the bulwarks of India against all invasions from the north and westward. It is fertile, it is healthful for Europeans, it is intersected with noble rivers, and a large portion of the inhabitants pant for the moment when the British troops will take the rule from out of the hands ot their oppressors. The JVluhomedans in Lahore are anxious that they should he governed bv Europeans. It is through that country that all invasions are apprehended, and the instant that it is known to the disaffected amongst the inhabitants of India that England is mistress ot the Funjaub they wifi succumb. In the meantime the Governor General has ordered the collecting on the frontiers of the Lahore kingdom of an army of 30,000 men at ditfurent points, yet so as to be concentrated immediately in casean emergency should arise Scinde continues perfectly peaceable throughout We have not heard (savs the Bombay Times) whether any attempts at collection ol revenue have been made, or if the tranquillity amounts to no more than tins, that the people are not inclined to meddle with us so long as we let them alone. The unusual fall ol rain, and extent ot the inundation, have been followed by the ordinary consequence þÿ an extraordinarily sickly season.

The news from Gabon! is confused and contradictory. Dost Mahoouned, it appears, finds it more difficult than ever to govern tire unruly Affghans. His notorious son Akbbar has, it is said, expressed bis dissatisfaction, as he says his father is þÿ too fond of the þÿEnglish. There is a chance of a collision with the Sikhs on account of the province of Peshawur, which the Affghans arc desirous of governing once more. Gandahar is represen ted as the scene of intrigues carried on by Persians. The conduct of the Schah of Persia is considered to be suspicious, and report spoke ol the probability of some hostile movement on the part of the British government, such as the re occupation of Karrak The Llio brig has taken the political agents to their posts at Bushire and Bagdad. I he Army of Lxereise on the Jumna has had the Generals and the Staff appointed, and was expected to come into operation before the close of this year. Lord Ellenborough continued at Barrackpore, near Calcutta, but it was expected that he would proceed to the noith western provinces, ft appears that the Sikhs have placed guards at the different forts, to prevent news of what is going on at Lahore from reaching the English. It is evidently a politic act on the part of Lord Ellenborough not to move from Calcutta until all his measures are matured, for his journey will excite greater alarm and disturbances at Gvvalior, and perhaps even in the Punjaub. The Madras newspapers state the death of Sir John Norton on board ship, while goiter

to Singapore for the benefit of his health. The treasure taken at Hyderabad had been brought to Bombay ; it amounts to about 700,000/, including the value of the jewels. One of the Ameer family, a vourig and ignorant man, had been brought by a steamer to Bombay, and sent to join the others at Sapoor, near Poonah.

An Indian Trnjrprfy. (From the Rochester Democrat.) Michigan, Nov. 7 þÿ The following Indian trageoj is related to me by Mr. James Fowls of this place. It occurred in this vicinity, all the parties being his neighbours; þÿ Nogisqua, an Indian of the Potowatamy tribe, residing in this vicinity, having pa wned bis gun and part of his clothing, from time to time, to a man named John N þÿ , for intoxicating drink, the trader proposed to the Indian that if he would sell him a certain cream coloured pony belonging to his squaw, and a present from her father (Bawbish. a chief of their tribe), he would give him up his gnu and clothing, and let him have more strong drink from time to time until the price agreed upon was paid. To this Nogisqua ngteed, and privately gave up the ponv, which was sent off further west. His squaw having gome suspicion of what Was going on, employed her younger brother to watch the result and inform her; which it appears he did. Upon the return ot the Indian to his camp partly intoxicated, his squaw, highly enraged, accused him of selling her pony. She became more and more enraged at Ins indifference about the .affair, and at length declared she would kill him. He handed her his scalping knife, and, drawing aside his hunting shirt, and making his bosom hare, coolly þÿexclaimed, þÿKinapoo! þÿ( Kill squaw. away.') She instantly plunged it in the þÿIndian b s reast, causing his death in-a few minutes. Her lather, the Indian chief, being then absent some 20 or 30 miles east, a

runner was despatched to inform him. Soon after, Mr, Fowle says, he saw him pass by his house with a sad countenance, lor the place of the murder. A heartrending duty now devolved upon the old chief. His word was to acquit or condemn his daughter, according to Indian I
